extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, in-house counsel, and applicants prosecuting patents at the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS)
extracted.subtask_short: Singapore patent prosecution and ex parte
extracted.subtask_description: Practice-note guidance on filing, prosecution, post-grant amendment, and ex parte re‑examination of patents before IPOS, including procedural requirements, substantive patentability standards, and strategic considerations for applicants and third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (section 13 Patents Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an invention to be patentable, it must be novel, involve an inventive step, and be capable of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to methods of treatment of the human or animal body by surgery or therapy, or of diagnosis practised on the human or animal body are not capable of industrial application and are not permitted (section 16). Patentability analysis follows IPOS Examination Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented invention standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-implemented inventions may be patentable if the computer or other technical features defined in the claims are integral to the invention and constitute the actual contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technical features should interact with the claimed steps (e.g., servers, databases, user devices) to a material extent and in a manner that addresses a specific problem. Merely reciting a generic computer or standard OS to perform a pure business method will not render it an invention (see sections 8.6 and 8.7, IPOS Examination Guidelines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality / public policy exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that may encourage offensive, immoral, or anti‑social behaviour will not be published and are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 13 of the Patents Act is cited; such subject matter will be excluded from publication and grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and extensions (section 36, 36A Patents Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: A granted patent is protected up to 20 years from the filing date, subject to renewal fees; term may be extended in limited situations (Registrar delay, regulatory delays for certain pharmaceuticals) by up to five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents publicly disclose details and may be exploited on expiry; statutory provisions specify extension circumstances (section 36A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing language and translation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Official filing language is English. Non-English direct national and PCT applications require an English translation and a verification of the English translation (VET) within prescribed timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-English direct national applications, submit English translation and VET within two months of Registrar's notification (rule 19(11)). For non-English PCT applications, submit English translation at filing and VET within two months from national phase entry due date (section 86(3)(a), rule 86(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing fees and timing (direct, divisional, national phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing fee must be paid within one month from submission of Patents Form 1 for direct national and divisional applications; for national phase entry, pay by the national phase entry due date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no electronic filing fee discount. Excess claims fees are charged upon filing a request for local substantive search/examination or on payment of fee for grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date and claims submission deadlines (section 17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective filing date is the date a complete application is filed or an earlier priority date. Claims are not required to obtain a filing date but must be submitted to the Registry within specified time limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit claims within 12 months after actual filing date if no priority; where priority claimed, submit claims within 12 months after declared priority date or two months after actual filing date, whichever later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available filing routes and national phase deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications may be filed as a direct national application (Domestic Route) or via PCT national phase entry. The national phase entry deadline is 30 months from earliest priority date or international filing date where no priority is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See sections 85 and 86, Patents Act and rule 86, Patents Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority entitlement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority date of an invention described in an application is the date of filing; where supported by matter in earlier applications, the priority date is the earliest filing date of the relevant earlier application(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPOS is not a participant in WIPO DAS; priority documents must be supplied by applicant per IPOS practice (see s.3.85 IPOS Examination Guidelines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period for certain disclosures (sections 14(4)(a)–(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A limited 12‑month grace period applies such that certain disclosures within 12 months before filing are disregarded as prior art if they resulted from specified breaches or displays or inventor presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifying disclosures include breaches of confidence, displays at certain international exhibitions, or presentations at a learned society; for direct national applications the 'date of filing' is the actual filing date (not earliest priority) for grace period calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for written authority to first‑file abroad (section 34)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Singapore resident wishing to first‑file a patent application outside Singapore must obtain written authority from the Registrar before filing abroad, unless specific exceptions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include where an application has been filed in the Registry at least two months before the foreign filing, or where no directions under section 33 apply (sections 33 and 34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficiency (section 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must disclose the invention clearly and completely so a person skilled in the art can perform it; application must include request for grant, specification, claims, any drawings referenced, and an abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirement: disclosure must be clear and complete; see rules 19, 21 and 22 and section 25 of the Patents Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims substantive requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must define the matter for which protection is sought; be clear and concise; be supported by the description; and relate to one invention or a group of inventions linked as a single inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must not rely on references to the description or drawings unless necessary for understanding or clarity (section 25, rule 19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims format options (two‑part or single statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be drafted in two parts (preamble + 'characterised in that' second part) or as a single statement setting out features of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two‑part format: first part indicates features necessary and part of prior art; second part states the technical features which, with first part, define protection sought. Multiple dependent claims are permissible in Singapore (sections 2.45, 2.46 IPOS Exam Guidelines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must be executed in black, white, or grayscale (no colour) and must not contain textual matter; features should be denoted by reference signs mentioned in description/claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See IPOS Patents Formalities Manual (section 2.2.16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor and right‑to‑patent rules (sections 24, 49, 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors have the right to be noted on any patent granted and on published applications where possible; the right to the patent primarily belongs to the inventor(s) but may belong to others by law or contract (e.g., employer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include employer ownership where invention developed in course of employment; succession in title also recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of local representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may appoint an advocate & solicitor or registered patent agent in Singapore to act on their behalf for proceedings before the Registrar and other matters under the Patents Act or related treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See sections 93, Patents Act and Rule 90, Patents Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing (section 27)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application is published in the Patents Journal 18 months from the effective filing date after a filing date has been accorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Journal is obtainable from IPOS Patent Journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary examination for formal requirements (section 28)
rubrics_metrics.description: On filing, a preliminary examination for compliance with formal requirements is conducted; Registrar notifies applicant if formal requirements are complied with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formalities check preceding substantive search/examination requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and examination request options and timelines (section 29, rules 38, 43)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may request (a) a search report within 13 months from effective filing date followed by an examination report within 36 months, or (b) an examination report (or search & examination report) within 36 months from effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain options require submission of final international search results or corresponding application search results and copies of documents referred to in those results. There is no general duty to disclose prior art to IPOS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome notices and review procedure (sections 29A, 29B, 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: After search/exam, Registry issues either notice of eligibility to proceed to grant or notice of intention to refuse based on objections; applicant may request review within two months with submissions or amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If notice of eligibility issued, applicant can request grant within two months. If review results in unresolved objection, notice of refusal issued and application deemed refused two months from notice. Multiple written opinions may be issued depending on unresolved objections and time to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third‑party observations rules (section 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication and before issuance of search/exam report, third parties may file written observations on patentability, stating reasons and providing supporting documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners consider only the documents submitted by the third party; reasoning should include accurate features mapping to claims and documentary support. Observations after establishment of search/exam report are placed on record but not forwarded to Examiner. Third‑party observations were formally introduced on 1 Oct 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment restriction during prosecution (section 84)
rubrics_metrics.description: No amendment may be made if it results in the application disclosing matter extending beyond that disclosed in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary amendments allowed before filing certain requests (search/exam/search&exam or review) and as part of response to written opinions. Two or more written opinions may be issued depending on unresolved objections and timing (rule 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application entitlement and timing (section 26(11), rule 27)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisional applications may be filed in respect of any part of matter in the earlier application before payment of fee for grant or before earlier application is refused/withdrawn/abandoned; divisional gets same filing date as earlier application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisional must be filed before certain terminal events for the earlier application (fee for grant, refusal, withdrawal, abandonment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrar's limitations on post‑grant amendments (section 84(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑grant amendments cannot result in the specification disclosing additional matter or extend the protection conferred by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrar assesses post‑grant amendments on sufficiency of disclosure, any unreasonable delay (circumstances, length, explanation), and whether patentee gained unfair advantage by delay (Warner‑Lambert considerations). Rule 52 sets out post‑grant amendment procedure; Form 17 required with full reasons and supporting evidence. Advertisement and opposition procedure apply (rules 52(1A)–52(9)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of allowed post‑grant amendment on enforcement (section 69(4), 70(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: If specification amended, courts will not award damages or other relief for infringement before the amendment unless satisfied the original specification was framed in good faith with reasonable skill and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where patent only partially valid, relief is discretionary and subject to proof of good faith and reasonable skill in drafting the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑grant re‑examination (section 38A) — ex parte nature and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may request re‑examination of a granted patent at any time, but re‑examinations are ex parte and the requester does not become a party; only the patentee is a party to re‑examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrar must refuse frivolous, vexatious or abuse requests, and no re‑examination allowed where validity is already in issue in pending court/Registrar proceedings (section 38A(4)–(5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for re‑examination (section 38A(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Re‑examination may be requested on grounds including: invention not patentable; specification does not disclose sufficiently; matter disclosed in specification extends beyond that in the application as filed; specified amendments or corrections that improperly add matter or extend protection; patents duplicate with same priority filed by same party; or other statutory grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional enumerated statutory scenarios (sections 20(3), 26(11), 47(4), 116(6) historical transitional provisions) and examples (incorrect corrections under section 107, improper amendments under section 31) are cited; requester must identify grounds specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re‑examination filing requirements and supporting evidence (rule 52A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Request must be filed on Patents Form 36 with official fee (SGD900) and a statement identifying each ground relied on, explaining how each ground is satisfied, and including relevant documents (with translations and VETs where needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement should identify the claims affected and state full reasons for each claim. Prior art should be dated (when made available to public). Supporting documents need not be limited to prior art (e.g., evidence that priority claims are invalid). If prior art was previously considered by Examiner, it must be presented in a new light with material new argument or interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re‑examination process milestones and patentee's limited response opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: If Registrar grants request, an Examiner reviews and issues a written opinion to patentee; patentee may request an interview within two months (agenda and any proposed amendments must be supplied), and must file a response within three months using Patents Form 13A containing written submissions or an application to amend (or both). There is only one opportunity to respond to the written opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After patentee response, Examiner prepares re‑examination report considering submissions and proposed amendments and any opposition statements to proposed amendments. Failure to respond makes the written opinion the re‑examination report (rule 52A(9)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re‑examination outcomes and remedies (sections 38A(11)–(14))
rubrics_metrics.description: If re‑examination report contains unresolved objections, Registrar must order either unconditional revocation or conditional revocation (revocation unless specification amended under section 83 to Registrar's satisfaction). Conditional revocation allows proprietor a final opportunity to amend; failure to amend results in full revocation. Revocation takes effect from date of grant. Patentee may appeal to High Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conditional revocation arises, amendments typically involve limiting claims to those deemed valid. Appeal available to General Division of High Court (section 90(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations for patentees regarding amendments and re‑examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees should proactively evaluate merits/strength of Singapore patents, consider prior art from other jurisdictions as soon as it becomes known, and apply promptly for post‑grant amendments to address potential invalidity before licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undue delay may preclude amendments (Warner‑Lambert). Post‑grant amendment may affect remedies in infringement proceedings; courts may deny relief if specification not framed in good faith and with reasonable skill. For third parties, re‑examination is quicker and cheaper but ex‑parte, whereas revocation proceedings are inter‑partes and allow fuller adversarial resolution (pleadings, evidence, cross‑examination).
